title: Supply Chain Scheduler, FIFO Under Constraints
description: A production scheduler for plastic bottle manufacturing: purchase orders queued FIFO, per-line capacity constraints, material availability windows, ETA computation, and a five-state fulfillment model that makes status readable.

lines.text: Two customers order bottles. Both need delivery Friday. One production line. One shift.
Whoever ordered first.
FIFO, yes. But what if order one needs material that arrives Thursday? Now scheduling, materials, and customer expectations collide.
What if both orders use different production lines?
Then capacity constraint relaxes but material availability may still block one of them.
Real factories juggle multiple lines, multiple materials, and shifting priorities simultaneously.

sections.title: What does the factory actually need?

lines.text: Project tracks purchase orders and supply orders for a bottle manufacturer.
Purchase orders are demands. Supply orders are raw material deliveries.
Core computation: given FIFO ordering, per-line capacity, material arrival dates, compute ETA and fulfillment status.
Five states: completed, in production, pending, delay expected, unable to fulfill.
Five states, not just done or not done?
Operations needs triage granularity. Delay expected means proactive customer outreach. Unable means escalate today.
System serves two audiences: operations needs scheduling truth, sales needs customer communication.
Five-state model gives sales actionable language: pending means not started yet, delay expected means proactive outreach required.
Who sets the line capacities and material lead times?
Operations configures them. System treats them as parameters, not hardcoded constants.
Per-line capacity means fixed units per day. One-liter and one-gallon lines differ.
Materials: PET resin, PTA, EG must be on site before production starts.
Scheduler processes purchase orders in submission order, checking feasibility at each step.
Blocked materials cause cascade delays: order two could start but waits behind blocked order one.
Should order two jump ahead? Strict FIFO wastes capacity. Priority scheduling complicates fairness.
Implementation chooses strict FIFO and documents that trade-off explicitly.
Scheduler processes orders in FIFO submission order but checks feasibility at each step.
Feasibility check has two parts: material availability at proposed start date, and remaining line capacity in the delivery window.
If PET resin arrives Tuesday and order proposes Wednesday start, material check passes.
If line already committed through Friday for earlier orders, capacity check fails. Order waits.
Cascade effect: order behind blocked order cannot jump ahead in strict FIFO even though its materials are ready.
Trade-off documented: strict FIFO maximizes fairness but wastes idle capacity. Priority-based maximizes throughput but complicates fairness.
Could you implement priority classes? Rush versus standard?
Yes, but then rush orders starve standard ones indefinitely during high demand. Need starvation prevention mechanism.
Prototype keeps strict FIFO for simplicity. Priority queues are documented as future enhancement with trade-off analysis.
Order one: ten thousand one-liter bottles submitted Monday. PET resin arrives Tuesday. Line capacity five thousand per day.
Production Wednesday through Thursday. ETA Thursday.
Order two: eight thousand one-gallon submitted Tuesday. Different line, capacity three thousand. Materials ready. Starts Tuesday, completes Friday.
Order three arrives Wednesday needing PET delayed to Monday. Status delay expected with computed slip.
Order four exceeds remaining window capacity. Unable to fulfill.
Detailed schedule computation walk-through.
Monday: purchase order PO-two-zero-two-six-zero-zero-three arrives for ten thousand one-liter bottles. Delivery due following Friday.
PET resin supply order SO-zero-zero-one scheduled to arrive Tuesday. Line capacity five thousand daily.
Material check for Tuesday start: resin arriving Tuesday, so earliest production start Wednesday. Two production days needed.
Line available Wednesday and Thursday. Schedule confirmed. ETA Thursday. Status transitions from pending to in-production on Wednesday.
Tuesday afternoon: purchase order PO-two-zero-two-six-zero-zero-four arrives for eight thousand one-gallon bottles. Different line, capacity three thousand daily.
Materials already on site for one-gallon production. Line available Tuesday. Three production days: Tuesday Wednesday Thursday. Completes Thursday.
Wednesday: PO-two-zero-two-six-zero-zero-five arrives needing PET resin but supply delayed to next Monday.
Status becomes delay expected. System computes revised ETA based on new material arrival plus production duration.
Friday: PO-two-zero-two-six-zero-zero-six arrives. Delivery due Monday. Required production exceeds remaining weekend capacity.
Status unable to fulfill within requested window. Sales team notified to negotiate new deadline with customer.
Line rates: five thousand one-liter daily. Three thousand one-gallon daily.
Material lead times: PET resin typically five to seven days from supplier.
Scheduler recomputes on every new order and every supply update.
Utilization metric: committed hours divided by available hours per line per week.
Above ninety percent leaves no buffer for breakdowns or rush orders. Dashboard displays all statuses simultaneously.
Key operational numbers.
One-liter line: five thousand units per day, single shift. One-gallon line: three thousand units per day.
PET resin lead time from supplier: five to seven business days typical. PTA and EG similar ranges.
Current utilization on one-liter line: two committed orders consuming four production days out of ten available weekly.
Utilization percentage: forty percent. Plenty of buffer for rush orders or equipment downtime.
Dashboard refreshes on every order creation and supply update. No batch processing delay.
Purchase orders queue FIFO. Supply orders track material arrivals.
Scheduler walks queue checking availability and capacity. Fit gets scheduled with computed dates.
Blocked on materials waits. Beyond window capacity becomes unable. Others show expected delay.
Dashboard displays live status for operations and sales.
Complete system pass.
Purchase orders queue FIFO. Supply orders track material arrival dates and quantities.
Scheduler walks queue checking material availability and line capacity at each proposed start date.
Feasible orders get scheduled with computed start and end dates. Blocked orders wait with reason recorded.
Orders exceeding window capacity become unable. Others with material delays become delay expected.
Dashboard displays all five statuses with utilization metrics for operational visibility.
Supply delivers early but system not updated. Orders stuck pending despite physical stock. Fix barcode scan at receiving.
Rush order bumped manually without documentation. Other orders slip mysteriously. Fix override requires reason code and audit trail.
Line breakdown halves capacity for week. All ETAs suddenly optimistic. Fix adjustable capacity parameter with effective dating.
Pending: customer notification SLA? Penalty clauses? Firm supplier commitments? Who owns fairness-versus-utilization trade-off?
More operational failure modes.
Supplier delivers wrong material grade. System shows PET on site but production line rejects it.
Signal: production starts late despite system showing ready. Fix barcode verification at receiving dock confirming grade.
Rush order manually overrides FIFO without documentation.
Signal: other orders slip mysteriously with no explanation. Fix override requires reason code and audit trail entry.
Production line breaks down mid-run. Half-completed batch sits idle.
Signal: all downstream ETAs shift. Fix adjustable effective-dated capacity parameter allowing temporary reduction.
Pending: automated customer notification on status change? Penalty clauses? Supplier firm-date commitments? Fairness-versus-utilization governance?
Can scheduler explain WHY delayed, naming the blocking constraint?
Recompute after supply change gives consistent results?
Can operations see per-line utilization and act before bottleneck?
Fourth: if you remove one supply order, does the scheduler correctly recalculate all dependent downstream orders?
Fifth: can sales answer where is my order without calling operations?
Self-test: order A submitted Monday needs material Thursday. Order B submitted Tuesday has material now. Who goes first and why?
Next time: document-to-HTML pipeline with staged processing and error recovery.
What about multi-stage manufacturing where bottles need labeling after molding?
Adds dependency chains between production stages. Significant complexity increase. Worth exploring separately.
